details: Existing agent benchmarks trade away realism, industry breadth, or automated verifiability, so benchmark gains do not track economically meaningful professional work; economically grounded alternatives (GDPval, RLI) rely on expensive human grading and cover few occupations.

ALE: a benchmark of ~960 expert-authored long-horizon professional task workflows (~1,490 runnable instances) spanning 55 digital subdomains / 13 clusters derived from the SOC 2018 + O*NET occupational taxonomy, contributed by 250+ practitioners as projects they had already completed.

Crux: every heterogeneous real-world deliverable is made automatically checkable without human judges, by standardizing scoring around deterministic artifact comparisons against expert references (exact/hashed values, tabular manifests with tolerances, geometric surface distances, replayed world state, executable tests) composed via a gate-and-score pattern, with LLM judging restricted to narrow evidence-anchored yes/no probes.

Each instance is an executable task specification (load/start/evaluate lifecycle) over a provisioned VM with an input//software//output//reference/ contract, decoupling task, agent, and environment; targets the 'Generalist Computer-Use Agent' class that interleaves GUI and CLI action in one loop.

Five-gate pipeline: expert sourcing via advisory committee, portal submission (description, input files, target software, expected deliverable, evaluation spec), conference-style first-pass review, engineer implementation with dry-runs, final peer-review QC checking reference correctness and tolerance calibration.
Admission criteria: representativeness (professionals' actual software), complexity (end-to-end deliverable taking days/weeks, not a single UI action), verifiability.
Contamination control: only 150 of 1,490 instances public, rest private, with planned rolling rotation; public subset validated as representative (Pearson r=0.89 vs full pool per cluster).
Taxonomy derived by LLM-assisted screening of 1,016 O*NET occupations down to 117 SOC base codes, 51 SOC-anchored subdomains plus 4 frontier subdomains.
152 public task instances split into three tiers: Near-Term (67), Full-Spectrum (55, one per subdomain), Last-Exam (38); plus ALE-CLI, a 105-task Linux-only subset.
Runs on GCP VMs (c4-standard-4 default, g2-standard-8 with L4 GPU for rendering/simulation), Linux or Windows targets; 5-hour wall-clock cap per run (3.8% timeout rate).
Metrics: full-pass rate and mean score in [0,1], plus API cost, wall-clock time, and token counts; scoring 93.2% code-based vs 6.8% LLM-judged, 88.5% host-side vs 11.5% VM-side verifiers.
All systems lifted to GCUA via GUI-as-Tool: a CUA MCP bridge exposing 14 desktop keyboard/mouse/screenshot tools inside the harness tool system (GUI-as-SubAgent reserved for non-vision models).

Harnesses: Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Droid, Gemini CLI, Grok CLI, OpenClaw, plus authors' ALE-Claw (Python re-implementation of OpenClaw's agent loop, ~65% smaller system prompt); CLI-only agents on ALE-CLI: ForgeCode, Hermes, Terminus, OpenHands.
Backbones: GPT-5.5/5.4, Claude Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8, Fable 5, Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Composer 2.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen3.6/3.7, GLM 5.1, Kimi K2.6, MiMo v2.5, MiniMax M2.7.
Factor decomposition: model sweep under fixed OpenClaw harness vs harness sweeps under fixed GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7 backbones.

Two-stage LLM failure analysis of Claude Code + Opus 4.7 failures: per-run analysis cards from logs, then GPT-4o classification into a two-level taxonomy (Understanding / Approach / Execution / Infrastructure).
Tool-call traces normalized into Bash/File/GUI/Web/Planning categories; domain-level score profiles; cost/time/token efficiency scatter.

key_findings.finding: ALE's hardest tier is essentially unsolved by all current frontier agent configurations.
key_findings.evidence: On the 38-task Last-Exam tier, average full-pass rate is below 1% across configurations; the best configurations (ALE-Claw/Cursor/Droid) reach only 2.6% pass and ~11-13% mean score, while Codex+GPT-5.5, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI record 0.0% pass. Overall public-set pass rates top out at 24.0% (Codex+GPT-5.5).

key_findings.finding: ALE tasks are substantially harder than existing terminal-centric benchmarks at comparable scale.
key_findings.evidence: Codex with GPT-5.5, which scores 82% on Terminal-Bench, reaches only 23.3% overall on the 105-task Linux-only ALE-CLI subset (37.2% Near-Term, 19.0% Full-Spectrum, 0.0% Last-Exam).

key_findings.finding: Backbone model choice dominates harness engineering as a driver of agent performance.
key_findings.evidence: Swapping the model under a fixed OpenClaw harness spans 16.8 pp of overall pass rate (4.3% Grok 4.3 to 21.1% GPT-5.5), roughly 3x the spread from swapping harnesses under a fixed backbone (4.9 pp for GPT-5.5 across five harnesses; 7.2 pp for Opus 4.7 across three).

key_findings.finding: Failures are dominated by domain understanding and planning rather than execution mechanics, and agents systematically avoid the intended domain GUI software.
key_findings.evidence: For Claude Code + Opus 4.7 failures, Approach errors account for 47% (wrong strategy 30%, abandoned 17%) and Understanding 31% (domain knowledge gap 25%, hallucination 6%), leaving 22% execution errors; meanwhile 34% of public instances designate graphical software as primary tool yet GUI tool-call share stays small as agents substitute Bash/CLI.

key_findings.finding: Higher resource spend does not buy better outcomes on ALE.
key_findings.evidence: ALE-Claw+GPT-5.5 attains the top overall mean score (45.8%) at $326, while the same harness with Opus 4.7 costs 3.6x more ($1,164) for 40.5%; Claude Code+Fable 5 spends $2,402 for 40.5%; Claude Code+Opus 4.8 needs 466 wall-clock hours for 37.2% versus ALE-Claw's ~51 hours; token-heavy runs (1,373M tokens) score below leaner ones (460M tokens).
